questions.question: A station reports 21 °C with a dew point of 18 °C. Explain why the gap between these two numbers tells you more than either number alone, and contrast it with a station reading 28 °C and 6 °C.
questions.expected_answer: The dew point is the temperature to which air must cool before it saturates and condensation begins, so on its own it is just a threshold. Compared with the air temperature it becomes a humidity gauge: the gap measures how much cooling stands between the air and saturation. At 21 °C with a dew point of 18 °C the gap is only three degrees — this air is nearly full of moisture, and a small amount of cooling, overnight or through uplift, will produce mist, cloud or drizzle; that narrow gap is typical of humid pre-frontal air. At 28 °C with a dew point of 6 °C the gap is twenty-two degrees: the air would need to shed twenty-two degrees before any condensation could begin, so it is very dry and clear conditions can be expected. Narrow gap means moist air and weather close at hand; wide gap means dry air — and quoting the gap with its numbers is what a complete answer requires.

questions.question: A bold toothed line crosses the chart. Describe the evidence, from the symbol and from stations on both sides, that would confirm it is a cold front, and state which way it is moving.
questions.expected_answer: The symbol itself: a cold front is a bold line set with solid triangles, and the triangles sit on the side the front is advancing toward — over South Africa they point north-east, since the front drives in from the south-west beneath a depression passing south of the country. Ahead of the line, north-eastern side, stations should show the pre-frontal signature: warm temperatures, a dew point crowding the air temperature, cloud thickening toward overcast, and a north-westerly wind feeding warm moist air in. Along the line itself, forced ascent of the warm air over the invading cold wedge builds a wall of cumulonimbus with heavy rain, gusts and lightning. Behind the line, stations report the transformation: sharply lower temperatures, wind swung to south-westerly, rising pressure and scattered showers giving way to clearing skies. A further fingerprint is that the isobars kink sharply where they cross the line. When symbol, pre-frontal stations, frontal cloud, post-frontal stations and kinked isobars all agree, the identification is proven rather than assumed.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of what the air masses are physically doing, why the weather changes so dramatically as a cold front passes a station.
questions.expected_answer: A cold front is the boundary where a mass of dense polar air, driving north-east, meets warm moist air. Because the cold air is denser, the two do not mix: the cold air slides in underneath and levers the warm air bodily off the surface. The lifted warm air cools rapidly by expansion, reaches its dew point, and releases its moisture in the towering cumulonimbus that ride along the front — hence the sudden darkening, gusts and downpour as the line passes. Once the front has gone through, the entire lower atmosphere at that station has been replaced: instead of warm humid air arriving on a north-westerly, cold polar air now covers the ground, blowing in as a south-westerly off the cold ocean, so temperature drops sharply — from around 21 degrees to perhaps 11. The depression the front was attached to moves away east and the next high-pressure cell builds in, so pressure rises. The cold air crossing still-warm land remains briefly unstable, giving cumulus and scattered showers, before subsiding air in the advancing high clears the sky. The drama, in short, is a wholesale exchange of one air mass for another, with violent uplift at the moving boundary.
